verdicts.trueWording: In this context detail is bad. It is trivia.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200, browser UA). Post 'The Swan Hollow Intrigue', posted September 5, 2026 by Bryce Lynch. Quote verbatim in the paragraph opening on the confusion between details and specifics; the same paragraph sets specificity against detail, so every limb (distinguishes detail from specificity; calls it trivia; says detail is bad) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: trying to recapture the campaign instead of the scenario
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). 'Ptolus: Running the Campaign - From Table to Page', January 5th, 2018, The Alexandrian. Quote verbatim; it is introduced as what you must be wary of when going table-to-page, i.e. adapting his own home campaign (The Complex of Zombies) into a publishable scenario, and the following paragraphs give the falls-in-love-with-an-NPC example. Warning limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: That IS the goal of good writing.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). 'The Lions of Tell Arn Part 2 - The City & The City', posted July 6, 2026 by Bryce Lynch. The sentence immediately follows his description of a designer who called up a mental image, lived the room, and got it on paper so the reading DM can pick it up and run it as imagined. Transfer limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: pads it like a school paper stretched to an assigned length
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200); the tag URL serves the full post 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', November 21, 2016, by David Hartlage. Quote verbatim in the section headed 'Longer descriptions', judging the 1989 Gamescience expanded Tegel Manor entry B9 BEDROOM against the shorter original. 'Expanded room description' and 'good middle sentence' limbs both on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Austere. Uncurtained windows let the gloomy light
verdicts.note:
Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). 'Bullet Points vs Prose', March 23, 2023, Luke Gearing. HTML confirms the layout: each room heading is followed by a

prose version and then a

    bullet version. Room '10) Study' prose opens with the one-word sentence 'Austere.' before the desk, dust and papers; the bullet twin instead opens 'Study - austere and spartan...'. One-word-first and before-inventory limbs both hold.

verdicts.trueWording: Use your outline (that is, your headings) to build a skeleton
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). 'Techniques to Write Adventures', September 14, 2021, Luke Gearing, under the heading 'Outline To Fuck'. The same sentence continues that your words, the details, are the meat; the following paragraph describes typing headings first in Markdown. Skeleton-first and words-as-meat limbs both supported.

verdicts.trueWording: presents his dungeon ideas as part of a coherent adventure
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). 'Part 46: "Zenopus Built a Tower"', Friday, February 6, 2015, section 'SAMPLE DUNGEON'. Page: the OD&D Sample Level is just a collection of examples whereas Holmes presents his dungeon ideas as part of a coherent adventure, almost a mini-setting. Both sides of the contrast are on the page. Attribution note: the post byline reads 'Zenopus Archives'; the name Zach Howard appears nowhere on the page (0 hits) and the Blogger profile does not render it, so the personal name rests on the source field, not this page.

verdicts.trueWording: here we at least get full English sentences describing each area

The sentence begins 'Rather than bullet-point atoms...', which carries the moved-from-bullet-points limb; the preceding section is the 1974 Castle Greyhawk bullet notes.

verdicts.trueWording: monster stat blocks grew too big to comfortably fit within the paragraph

Delta writes that he finds it interesting to pinpoint in this one document the moment when monster stat blocks grew too big to comfortably fit within the paragraph text and had to move to a dedicated place. Locates-the-moment limb explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: Room descriptions have important object in bold with parenthesis containing details

Praise limb explicit two lines earlier, where he calls the best text innovations those championed by the OSR with Old-School Essentials as his example; he then gives a worked room example with the bolded object and parenthetical detail.

verdicts.trueWording: a compact series of encounters appropriate for a specific level of play
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). 'Dungeon Delve: WTF?', The Alexandrian. The sentence sits in an indented block (padding-left/right 60px in the HTML) among the passages Alexander quotes from the Dungeon Delve introduction, which he introduces as written by Bill Slavicsek, WotC Director of R&D. The block continues that the book holds 30 Delves, one per level, three encounters each. Definition and attribution limbs both supported.

verdicts.trueWording: unless you hook the reader in the first half-page

'Let's Design an Adventure: Adventure Hooks and Opening Scenes', by Shawn Merwin, published 2019-10-23, section 'You May Ask Yourself, How Did I Get Here?'. Taught limb explicit: he frames it as one of the most sobering things he was told in his creative writing classes.
